opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is to make the boundary between the two less of a wall and more of a shared space. In a lot of organizations, the algorithm people think of infrastructure as a service: "I write the model, you make it run fast." And the infra people think of algorithms as a moving target: "Every week they change the architecture and break my kernels." Both sides are a bit right, and that's exactly the problem.

From my own experience working on inference systems like vLLM, the best progress happens when the same person, or at least the same small group, can hold both sides in their head. When you design a new attention variant, you should already be asking how the KV cache will be laid out and whether it can be batched efficiently. And when you build the serving system, you should understand why the researchers want something like a sliding window or a mixture of experts, not just treat it as a spec you were handed.

Practically, I'd suggest a few things. First, co-design should start early. Don't let the model architecture be frozen and then thrown over the fence. Have infra people in the room when the architecture decisions are made, because a small change there can mean a 2x difference in serving cost later.

Second, shared metrics. If the algorithm team is only judged on benchmark scores and the infra team only on throughput, they'll optimize against each other. Something like "quality per dollar" or "quality at a given latency" forces everyone to care about the same thing.

Third, good abstractions in the codebase itself. A lot of friction is really a software engineering problem. If adding a new model requires touching a hundred places in the infra code, researchers will avoid it or hack around it. If the system is modular and clean, a researcher can plug in a new idea themselves and see how it performs, and that builds empathy naturally.

And finally, culture: respect for the other side's work. Infra work is often invisible when it goes well. Organizations that celebrate a big efficiency win as much as a new model result tend to attract people who are willing to cross that boundary. In the end, at the frontier today, the model and the system are really one thing. The organizations that understand that will move much faster.

r001.rationale: The response recommends early co-design and having infrastructure people in architecture discussions, but does not clearly say that exposure to each other’s everyday discussions helps each team understand the other’s concerns.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention expert-choice routing or give an MoE load-balancing example where infrastructure priorities override algorithmic suitability.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that the gap between algorithm and infrastructure teams is not really a technical problem, it's a problem of incentives and of shared language.

From my experience working on vLLM, the healthiest dynamic is when the people who build the system are also the people who feel the pain when a model doesn't run well. When I was doing research at Tsinghua, I noticed that algorithm people tended to treat the infrastructure as a black box. They would write a model, hand it over, and if it was slow or didn't fit in memory, that was "someone else's problem." And on the infrastructure side, engineers would optimize kernels or scheduling in isolation, sometimes without really understanding why a model is structured the way it is, or which parts of the computation actually matter for the final quality.

So practically, I think there are a few things an organization can do.

First, rotate people. Let algorithm researchers spend real time, not a week but months, inside the infrastructure stack. Let infrastructure engineers sit in model training reviews. The point is not that everyone becomes an expert in everything, but that each side develops an intuition for the other's constraints. Once an algorithm person has personally debugged a CUDA out-of-memory error at 2 a.m., they design models differently.

Second, make the interface between the two teams explicit and measurable. A lot of friction comes from vague handoffs: "this model should be fast." Fast on what hardware, at what batch size, with what latency target? If you have shared benchmarks and shared dashboards that both teams look at every day, then the conversation becomes about numbers rather than about blame.

Third, and this is something I feel strongly about from open source: co-locate ownership. In vLLM, when a new model architecture comes in, the people adding it have to touch both the modeling code and the execution path. There is no clean wall between "the model" and "the engine." That forces integration to happen early, when it is cheap, rather than late, when it is painful.

And finally, leadership has to signal that infrastructure work is first-class. In many organizations, the algorithm team gets the papers and the credit, and the infrastructure team gets the on-call pages. If promotion and recognition only flow to one side, no amount of process will bring the teams together. People go where the respect is.

So in short: shared pain, shared metrics, shared ownership, and shared credit. If you get those four things right, the collaboration tends to follow naturally.

r001.rationale: The response recommends months-long rotations and having infrastructure engineers sit in model training reviews so each side understands the other’s constraints. This conveys the value of exposure to the other team’s work and discussions.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention expert-choice routing, MoE load balancing, or an example of infrastructure priorities overriding algorithmic suitability.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to give both teams a shared goal and a short feedback loop. If the algorithm team only focuses on model quality, and the infrastructure team only focuses on reliability or utilization, each team can do its job well while the overall system still performs poorly.

For example, when developing a model, bring infrastructure engineers into the discussion early. They can help explain which choices will be expensive to train or difficult to serve. At the same time, infrastructure engineers need to understand what the algorithm team is trying to achieve, so they can optimize the things that actually matter.

It also helps to have people work together on a concrete problem—say, reducing inference latency while preserving model quality. That creates a reason to share tools, measurements, and knowledge. You don’t necessarily need everyone to become an expert in both areas, but you do need enough shared understanding that they can make tradeoffs together.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to give both teams a shared goal and a short feedback loop. If the algorithm team only cares about model quality and the infrastructure team only cares about system performance, they can each do a good job locally while the overall product suffers.

A practical way to bring them together is to have them work on the same concrete problem—for example, improving model quality under a latency and cost constraint. Then they need to understand each other’s tradeoffs. The infrastructure engineers learn why a particular model feature matters, and the algorithm engineers learn what makes that feature expensive to serve.

You also want to make experimentation easy. If testing an idea requires weeks of coordination, people will work around each other. With shared benchmarks, good profiling tools, and regular conversations about actual bottlenecks, collaboration becomes part of the daily workflow.
